strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of existing story visualization paradigms (AR's error accumulation, RI's inability to capture emerging characters)
Elegant iterative framework design that leverages all previously generated images as references, providing principled approach to semantic consistency
Practical plug-and-play GRCA module that reduces computational costs while maintaining effectiveness compared to existing consistency methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFiD), diverse baselines, thorough ablations, and human evaluation showing consistent preference
Training-free approach that works with pre-trained models, making it practical and accessible
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines (9.4% on aCS vs. StoryDiffusion), particularly strong on long sequences
Clear presentation with effective figures and promising reproducibility through code release
Broader applicability demonstrated through subject-consistent generation comparisons
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—the iterative paradigm is a straightforward application of existing ideas; GRCA is essentially lightweight cross-attention using CLIP embeddings; linear weighting strategy is simplistic
Evaluation on long stories severely limited: only 20 curated GPT-4o-generated stories lacks statistical significance and diversity; no established long-story benchmark comparison
Human evaluation scope insufficiently specified (unclear number of raters, inter-rater agreement metrics, detailed evaluation protocol)
Incomplete computational analysis: while GRCA reduces FLOPs vs. CSA, lacks wall-clock time/memory comparisons; no analysis of practical runtime for 100-frame sequences
Insufficient failure case analysis—paper predominantly shows positive results with limited discussion of limitations, failure modes, or when method degrades
Hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc with limited sensitivity analysis (λ: 0.3→0.5 schedule lacks justification; Table 3 ablations incomplete)

Technical clarity issues: Equations 3-4 tensor operations under-specified; Algorithm 1 lacks implementation details on reference aggregation; GRCA memory implications with accumulating references not discussed
Method-specific limitations not addressed: requires explicit per-frame prompts; framework specific to diffusion models; no evaluation on diverse visual styles or complex narratives
Potential reference accumulation bias—accumulating all previous frames could bias toward early content; visual diversity degradation over story progression not analyzed
Reproducibility gaps: exact CLIP model version not specified; reference image selection/aggregation strategy under-specified

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID), human evaluation, and extensive ablation studies demonstrating thorough empirical validation
Well-motivated problem addressing concrete limitations of existing AR and RI paradigms in maintaining semantic consistency during long story visualization
Practical training-free approach that leverages existing pretrained models without requiring finetuning
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and generally well-written exposition of the methodology
weaknesses: Severely limited technical novelty: Core iterative refinement using previous frames is straightforward; GRCA is essentially standard cross-attention applied to global CLIP embeddings without fundamental innovation. The linear weighting strategy lacks principled justification

Marginal empirical improvements that fail to support claims of superiority: Regular-length stories show <1% gains over StoryDiffusion (0.315 vs 0.313 CLIP-T); long stories show <1% improvement in human evaluation (4.29 vs 4.25). These negligible differences undermine the paper's central claims

Approach closely mirrors StoryDiffusion with insufficient differentiation: Both methods use iterative refinement with previous frames as reference; the key distinction (GRCA vs CSA) appears incremental. The paper inadequately acknowledges this similarity or provides deep analysis of why GRCA specifically helps

Misleading 'training-free' characterization: Requires careful hyperparameter tuning (iteration count, λ schedule, diffusion steps, guidance scale). No sensitivity analysis provided; this contradicts the training-free framing

Computational efficiency not properly addressed: Figure 8 only shows single-image generation cost, not end-to-end story generation timing. The iterative paradigm requires multiple diffusion passes per frame, but no practical timing comparisons provided

Design choices lack theoretical justification: Why is the specific λ weighting schedule optimal? Why 10 iterations instead of 5? Why this initialization strategy? The paper shows these work but doesn't explain why, limiting insights
Narrow evaluation scope limited to single domain (story visualization from text) with single base model (Stable Diffusion), restricting generalizability and impact
Visual quality degradation in long stories inadequately addressed: Figures 12-14 show quality loss for very long stories (up to 100 frames) without principled solutions beyond more iterations

Insufficient mechanistic analysis: The paper doesn't explain why GRCA specifically improves consistency or identify failure modes. Missing analysis of performance scaling with story length and principled ablation of the weighting schedule itself

Training-free and practical approach applicable to different pre-trained diffusion models

Strong empirical results with consistent improvements over baselines (9.4% over StoryGen in aCS, 8.14 in aFID)
Effective presentation with clear visualizations and well-structured explanations
Systematic validation of iterative paradigm and GRCA components through ablation studies
Addresses real practical challenge in long story visualization with scalable solution

Narrow evaluation scope: only one primary dataset (StorySalon), 20 long story test cases, limited to English
Hyperparameter design lacks justification: linear weighting strategy appears ad-hoc with limited sensitivity analysis
Heavy reliance on CLIP-based and aCS metrics which have known limitations for evaluating semantic consistency; missing action/temporal coherence evaluation
Incomplete failure analysis: 'closed-eye issue' mentioned but not systematically analyzed; no discussion of failure modes beyond 100 frames
Unclear scaling behavior to much longer sequences; no analysis of error accumulation patterns or memory requirements for very long histories
Limited exploration of alternative design choices (e.g., non-linear weighting schemes, other attention aggregation methods)
Human evaluation protocol and sample size not clearly specified

strengths: Well-motivated iterative paradigm that addresses real limitations of auto-regressive and fixed reference-image approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (CLIP-T, aCS, aFID), large-scale testing (up to 100 frames), human evaluation, and detailed ablations
Consistent and meaningful improvements over strong baselines (9.4% CLIP-T improvement, 3.4% aCS, 3.14% aFID)
Training-free approach with no fine-tuning required, making it broadly applicable and practical
Clear presentation with good visualizations, pseudocode provided, and implementation details for reproducibility
Practical variants (Story-Iter-Fast, Story-Iter-ControlNet) demonstrating flexibility and applicability
Thorough ablation studies examining initialization, GRCA, and weighting strategies
weaknesses: Core novelty is limited - using all previous frames as references is a relatively straightforward idea; GRCA module primarily leverages existing techniques without significant innovation
Significant unresolved computational efficiency: 250 minutes for 100-frame generation severely limits practical applicability; even Story-Iter-Fast requires substantial computation
Fundamental and unresolved trade-off between consistency and text-image alignment (Table 11, Fig. 19): more iterations improve consistency but degrade alignment, suggesting inherent limitations
Acknowledged diversity limitation (Section G) with limited exploration of solutions or thorough analysis of the problem
Limited generalization analysis - evaluation primarily on StorySalon dataset with unclear transferability to other domains

Fine-grained interaction improvements over reference-image methods claimed but only supported by visual inspection, not quantitative validation

strengths: Clear problem formulation identifying limitations of existing Auto-Regressive and Reference-Image paradigms for long story visualization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 10+ baselines, multiple metrics (CLIP-T, aCCS, aFID), and ablation studies across key design choices
Extension of story visualization evaluation to 100-frame stories, contributing a useful benchmark for longer narratives
Well-motivated iterative paradigm using all previous frames as references, providing intuitive approach to maintaining global context
Extensive qualitative results demonstrating versatility across different story styles and lengths
Practical variants (Story-Iter-Fast, Story-Iter-ControlNet) showing engineering effort to address efficiency and controllability
Human evaluation across multiple dimensions (alignment, interaction, consistency, content) in addition to automatic metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: iterative refinement is straightforward, GRCA is essentially standard cross-attention, and linear weighting (λᵢ = λ₁ + ρ × (i-1)) is overly simplistic without principled design
Marginal quantitative improvements without statistical significance testing: CLIP-T improves <1% (0.318 vs 0.315), aCCS within 1-2 points, many gains appear within noise margins
Severe computational overhead not justified: ~2x cost (44.09 vs 22.32 TFLOPs) and 15 seconds per frame for <1% improvement makes practical deployment questionable

Fundamental consistency-alignment trade-off unresolved: Table 11 shows CLIP-T degrades with iterations (0.330→0.297) while aCCS improves, indicating competing objectives that cannot be simultaneously optimized

Experimental fairness concerns: inconsistent baseline setup, limited custom benchmark (6,026 prompts with 14 avg frames), qualitative-only evaluation for 100-frame stories, and no confidence intervals or significance testing
Human evaluation shows Story-IterXL achieves identical scores to Story-Iter (4.20/4.33), questioning whether the iterative paradigm provides meaningful practical value
Excessive paper length (31 pages) with many visualizations (Figs 24-33) that add limited scientific value; core contributions could be conveyed more concisely
Unresolved fundamental trade-offs: linear weighting insufficient to balance local diversity and global consistency; acknowledged but not adequately addressed
Metric and evaluation concerns: aFID and aCCS are relatively new metrics, CLIP-T may not ideally capture long-story coherence, human evaluation scale and inter-rater agreement unclear
Hyperparameter choices (λ₁=0.5, ρ=0.5) lack justification or systematic ablation; reproducibility limited by GPT-4o dependency for LLM refinement

strengths: Novel iterative paradigm that differs meaningfully from auto-regressive and reference-image approaches, with clear motivation and strong empirical benefits
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including multiple metrics (CLIP-T, aCS, aFID), extensive baseline comparisons, rigorous ablation studies, and both quantitative and human evaluation
Strong and consistent experimental results, achieving 9.4% CLIP-T improvement over baselines for regular stories and superior performance on long sequences up to 100 frames
Training-free approach using plug-and-play GRCA module, demonstrating practical applicability and generalizability across different base models
Introduces a new long-story visualization benchmark addressing an evaluation gap in the field
Excellent presentation and reproducibility with pseudocode, implementation details, and commitment to release code
Produces high-quality, visually coherent long-story generations with fine-grained details and semantic consistency across diverse styles
weaknesses: Computational efficiency remains a concern with 5 minutes required to generate 100-frame stories at 1024×1024, limiting practical deployment, and only incremental speedup gains from Story-Iter-Fast variant

Unresolved trade-off between global consistency and text-image alignment; more iterations improve semantic consistency but hurt CLIP-T scores, with only a simplistic linear weighting strategy proposed
Limited technical novelty in individual components—GRCA is essentially token aggregation with attention weighting, combining existing techniques rather than introducing fundamental innovations
Benchmark is relatively small with only 20 stories (10 in evaluation set) and limited diversity, insufficient as a standard for long-story visualization evaluation
Incomplete analysis of method design choices such as embedding flattening, n=4 token default, and insufficient exploration of alternative aggregation mechanisms for reference frames
Generalization testing limited to Stable Diffusion-based models; unclear how well the approach transfers to other diffusion architectures or vision-language models
Limited analysis of failure cases and how the method handles novel entities introduced mid-story; diversity loss acknowledged but not thoroughly explored

Evaluation metrics have limitations: aCS and aFID rely on object bounding boxes and may miss other consistency dimensions; CLIP-T may not reflect visual quality; human evaluation has modest sample sizes
